title: Privacy Enhancement Based on Quantum Key Distribution Protocols
abstract: This paper explores the integration of privacy enhancement techniques with Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols. We investigate the utilization of quantum teleportation and quantum state superposition to bolster the security of key distribution. The core concept involves combining the key distribution process with quantum teleportation and superposition, leveraging the properties of quantum entanglement and state superposition to achieve enhanced privacy. This approach aims to mitigate potential eavesdropping attacks by fundamentally altering the information exchange process. The theoretical framework presented here contributes to the growing body of research exploring secure communication paradigms in the quantum era. The primary objective is to demonstrate a viable methodology for significantly increasing the security of QKD systems, particularly against sophisticated attacks. The proposed method relies on the inherent unpredictability of quantum mechanics and the difficulties associated with intercepting and measuring quantum states without disturbing them. We present a detailed mathematical model illustrating the key aspects of the proposed protocol, focusing on the generation and distribution of a shared secret key while maintaining the confidentiality of the key itself.

title: Neural Symbolic Artificial Intelligence: A Knowledge Graph Reasoning Mechanism
abstract: This paper explores the integration of neural networks and symbolic reasoning within the emerging field of Neural Symbolic Artificial Intelligence (NeSyAI). The core challenge lies in effectively combining the knowledge representation and learning capabilities of neural networks with the logical inference and validation mechanisms of symbolic systems, particularly in the context of knowledge graph reasoning. We propose a novel mechanism – a neuro-symbolic reasoning engine – designed to bridge this gap. This engine leverages neural networks for representing and learning knowledge from knowledge graphs, while utilizing the graph structure for performing inference and ensuring the soundness of conclusions. This architecture addresses limitations of purely neural or purely symbolic approaches by providing a robust and explainable reasoning framework. The paper details the key components of this engine, focusing on the interplay between neural embeddings and logical rules, and outlines a potential framework for its implementation. Finally, we discuss the potential impact of this approach on various applications, including question answering, data integration, and automated reasoning. ---

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for Cryptography Cybersecurity in Uganda: Robustness Under Distribution Shift and Sparse Labels
abstract: The federated monitoring of cryptographic failure and cyber-intrusion signals across Ugandan institutions inherits two under-addressed tensions: client event distributions drift with sectoral traffic, software configuration and adversary behaviour, and attack labels remain sparse because cryptographic incident confirmation is slow, costly and legally sensitive. It combines local differential privacy with a distributionally robust semi-supervised objective over Wasserstein perturbations. The main results are a Kantorovich–Rubinstein bound relating tolerated distribution shift and loss variation, an excess-risk bound for confidence-thresholded pseudo-labelling under sparse labels, and a privacy-utility trade-off specified through Rényi differential privacy and secure aggregation. The framework distinguishes what can be guaranteed at design time from what must be validated by local security operations alone. The result is not an empirical report on Ugandan data; it is a mathematically stated protocol of assumptions, theorems and implementation conditions tailored to Uganda's inter-institutional cyber incident monitoring under the Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019.

title: Natural Language Processing and Text Analytics
abstract: Natural language processing (NLP) and text analytics have become tools for understanding how people use language and mining useful information from vast amounts of written text. These technologies combine language studies, computer science, and artificial intelligence in efforts to make machines capable of understanding, interpreting, and even creating language very similarly to how it is created by humans. Text analytics applies NLP methods that turn messy and disorganized text into clear, structured data to allow firms to find patterns, sentiments, and trends. Together, these technologies support many applications, including chatbots and recommendation systems, public opinion tracking, and reviewing legal documents. Recent improvements in deep learning and context-aware word representations have increased the capabilities of machines in understanding the meaning and subtleties of language. This chapter investigates the basics, steps, and challenges of NLP and text analytics that make them crucial in today’s world for generating new ideas and making good decisions.

title: The quantum switch as a commutation-syndrome filter for qubit Pauli channels: deterministic advantage over definite-order strategies and an exact geometric law
abstract: Abstract The quantum switch is known to remove noise probabilistically, but whether this constitutes an advantage over causally ordered processing has remained contentious: postselection, weak classical benchmarks, and task-dependent comparisons have all drawn criticism. Here we give an exact analysis of the question for a qubit under Pauli noise. For any two qubit Pauli channels, measuring the switch’s control qubit implements a commutation syndrome : it sorts each noise realization by whether the two Kraus errors commuted, syndrome information that an unencoded qubit does not otherwise possess, and the optimal measure-and-feed-forward protocol has a closed form. The analytical results have two levels of generality. For the exactly solvable pair, an isotropic depolarizing channel and a flip channel along an arbitrary axis, we prove a complete ceiling theorem: every definite-order protocol using each channel once, with arbitrary memoryless intermediate operations and receiver-side post-processing, deterministic or heralded, has entanglement fidelity at most ma x P c P , and the switch exceeds this ceiling deterministically , by p q / 3 over most of parameter space. For arbitrary qubit Pauli pairs, the ceiling is proven against arbitrary receiver-side post-processing, and the gain is strictly positive if and only if the two syndrome branches call for different Pauli corrections, confining the exceptions to error-dominated noise. Side systems are covered whenever they are non-signaling about the message. Beyond these theorems the evidence is numerical: strict gain in 99.8 % of 5000 random Pauli pairs, and no case, within a 200 -pair sample, in which an optimized midpoint echo overturns the gain. The state-resolved gain obeys an exact geometric law, Δ F = 2 p q / 3 | r ^ ⋅ n ^ | 2 : alignment is the condition under which the degenerate two-error syndrome becomes perfectly correctable. The separation survives control dephasing down to a threshold visibility that falls with noise strength, and at strong noise it outperforms coherent control of the two orderings even with twice the channel uses.

title: Storing Infinite Dynamical Attractors in Nonreciprocal Associative Neural Networks
abstract: We develop a dynamical mean-field theory for nonreciprocal associative networks that store an extensive number of dynamical attractors, from limit cycles to strange attractors. Using a path integral calculation under quenched disorder, we derive self-consistent dynamical mean-field equations for pattern overlaps, autocorrelations and response functions. Memory retrieval capacity is governed by the spectral structure of the coupling matrices encoding stored patterns. When their eigenvalues are coherently aligned, retarded self-interactions and quenched noise feed back destructively: at zero eigenphase (fixed point attractors) the classical equilibrium capacity bound is recovered, while for limit cycles retrieval collapses far below it. In contrast, for uniformly distributed eigenphases, retarded self-interactions and much of the quenched noise cancels, reducing the dynamics to an effective single-spin process and amplifying capacity substantially. We validate the theory against microscopic simulations for limit-cycle and chaotic attractors, identifying eigenvalue decoherence as the mechanism enabling enhanced storage of dynamical memories.

title: Extracting Voice Styles from Frozen TTS Models via Gradient-Based Inverse Optimization
abstract: Some text-to-speech systems ship a synthesis model and preset style vectors but withhold the reference encoder that turns a recording into a style vector, so a user cannot obtain a style for a new voice. We recover that vector without the encoder by inverting the released pipeline with gradient descent: all weights stay frozen and only the style vector is optimized, against time-pooled WavLM statistics of one recording of the target. The objective discards the time axis, so no transcript is needed. Two constraints from the release make the result a drop-in style: every row of the timbre style stays on the unit sphere where the presets lie, and the small duration style, which a time-pooled loss cannot see, is fitted to the recording's speaking rate. On SupertonicTTS, over 147 speakers and 100 held-out sentences each, ECAPA-TDNN similarity rises from 0.129 to 0.419, every recovered style starts from a preset and ends closer to its target than that preset was, and the pooled word error rate stays below that of the presets. A verifier at its equal-error point accepts 52% of the recovered voices as the target speaker, against 1% of the presets.

title: Dimension Generalization with Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper investigates the integration of dimensionality generalization and quantum entanglement to achieve highly accurate geometric modeling. The core claim is to develop a novel method leveraging quantum entanglement to map low-dimensional spaces to higher-dimensional spaces, utilizing entanglement for precise geometric calculations and enabling high-precision modeling. We propose a quantum computing algorithm designed to perform geometric computations within low-dimensional spaces, guided by the entangled states generated by this process. This approach offers a fundamentally new pathway for geometric data analysis and modeling, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical techniques. The paper explores the potential of this combination to address challenges in geometric representation and precise calculation, highlighting the key mechanisms involved and outlining future research directions.

title: Wave Function Collapse for Bayesian Inference in Complex Systems
abstract: This paper explores the application of wave function collapse (WFC) to Bayesian inference within complex systems. We propose a novel algorithm that leverages quantum superposition to efficiently explore multiple possible states simultaneously, aiming to improve the accuracy of Bayesian inference across a wider range of problems. The core mechanism centers around dynamically collapsing wave functions based on a probabilistic assessment of the system's state, mitigating the limitations of traditional methods. We detail the algorithm's design, provide an example demonstrating its efficacy, and discuss potential future directions, including scalability and application to diverse complex systems.

title: Adam Prism: A Sovereignty-First Architecture for Verified, Deterministic LLM Agents
abstract: Autonomous LLM agents that generate code, documents, or system artifacts face a structural problem: their outputs are stochastic, while the environments they must produce for are deterministic. Orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen move control out of the model loop, yet verification still relies on LLM-as-a-judge. We present Adam Prism, a sovereignty-first agent architecture that treats verification as a first-class architectural layer. Planning, execution, verification, and repair are separated into independent stages; a deep-verification loop combines deterministic functional checks with an independent spec-conformance judge; and a bounded escalation ladder repairs defects with an honest stop. On a local 12B model via Ollama the system sustains 1,317 deterministic tests and 26 scenario workflows, and two independent oracle-checked registries (10 CSV-verification and 5 code-generation scenarios) reach 10/10 and 15/15 (100%) single-shot --- zero cost, air-gap capable. This package contains the paper, its sources, and the measured benchmark data. No source code is included.

title: Quantum Error Correction Protocols: A Topology-Enhanced Reinforcement Learning Approach
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is a critical component of quantum computing, enabling reliable transmission and manipulation of quantum information. Current QEC protocols, particularly surface codes, suffer from inherent vulnerabilities to information loss due to noise and imperfections in the hardware. This paper introduces a novel quantum error correction protocol utilizing topology-enhanced reinforcement learning (TEL) to mitigate these risks. The core concept is to model the quantum error correction process as a dynamically evolving topological structure, effectively reducing the vulnerability to information leakage. We propose a TEL-based algorithm that leverages the inherent properties of topological spaces to guide the optimization process, leading to improved error correction capabilities. This research presents a preliminary investigation of the algorithm's effectiveness through simulations and a simplified, illustrative example. The presented approach offers a promising pathway towards robust and efficient QEC, potentially simplifying the development of practical quantum systems.

title: 基于自适应拓扑的量子计算的能量筛选
abstract: This paper investigates the application of adaptive topology in quantum computing to enhance energy selection within quantum algorithms. Traditional quantum algorithms often struggle with computationally expensive energy calculations, necessitating the identification and elimination of high-energy states. We propose a novel quantum computation paradigm centered around dynamically adjusting computational parameters based on a self-organized topological structure. This approach allows for rapid and efficient energy screening, potentially leading to significant improvements in quantum algorithm performance. The core mechanism involves constructing a topology that reacts to the energy landscape of a quantum system, effectively prioritizing the propagation of energy along specific paths. This paper details the theoretical framework, simulation results, and potential implications of this innovative approach.

title: Dynamic Topology for Geometric Information Compression
abstract: This paper explores the application of dynamic topology to geometric information compression. Geometric information, traditionally represented as complex data structures, often requires significant storage and transmission. We propose a novel algorithm that leverages dynamic topology, a mathematical framework that allows for continuous structural changes, to compress data. The core mechanism involves constructing and manipulating a dynamic topological structure that effectively encodes the geometric properties of the input data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through rigorous analysis and simulations, showcasing significant improvements in compression ratios compared to existing methods. The algorithm's efficiency stems from its ability to adapt to the data's inherent structure, allowing for higher compression rates. Furthermore, the dynamic nature of the topology ensures a more robust compression process.

title: Context-Aware Neural Turing Machines with Episodic Memory
abstract: This paper introduces a novel architecture, Context-Aware Neural Turing Machines with Episodic Memory (CAN-ETM), designed to address the limitations of existing Neural Turing Machines (NTMs) regarding contextual understanding and long-term dependency learning. Current NTMs struggle to effectively incorporate surrounding context, leading to difficulties in tasks requiring temporal reasoning and complex pattern recognition. Our proposed solution integrates an episodic memory module with the NTM, enabling the network to store and retrieve past experiences based on contextual cues derived from the current input. This mechanism facilitates the learning of more intricate and nuanced temporal patterns. The core claim is that augmenting NTMs with this contextual episodic memory significantly enhances their ability to model sequential data. We demonstrate this through a theoretical framework outlining the key components and their interactions, and propose a set of equations to illustrate the learning process. The CAN-ETM architecture represents a significant step forward in building more intelligent and adaptable neural network models for tasks involving context-dependent learning.

title: Multi-Agent Simulation with Emergent Social Norms using Agent-Based Modeling
abstract: This paper explores the use of agent-based modeling (ABM) to simulate the emergence of social norms within a population of autonomous agents. The core idea is that complex social behaviors, including the formation of norms, can arise from the interactions of agents following simple, rule-based behaviors. This research provides a framework for investigating how social norms develop in dynamic systems, offering a method to understand phenomena such as cooperation, altruism, and even conflict. The simulation presented utilizes a discrete event-based ABM environment where agents possess attributes like trust, reputation, and observational capabilities. Agents interact based on a set of predefined rules, and the accumulated interactions lead to the statistically observable emergence of norms. The model's parameters, including agent attributes, interaction probabilities, and the influence of observation, are varied to demonstrate the sensitivity of norm formation to these factors. The results demonstrate the potential of ABM to capture emergent social dynamics and provide insights into the underlying mechanisms driving norm formation. Further research will explore the robustness of these norms and their impact on system-wide behavior.

title: Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) for Accelerating Machine Learning
abstract: The burgeoning field of machine learning (ML) is increasingly reliant on massive datasets for training complex models, particularly deep neural networks. However, the retrieval of data from conventional memory systems represents a significant bottleneck, limiting the scalability and efficiency of ML algorithms. This research proposes a Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) architecture designed to overcome this limitation by leveraging quantum mechanical principles. The core concept involves encoding data into qubits and utilizing quantum random access to achieve near-instantaneous data retrieval. This paper details a novel QRAM architecture, focusing on qubit arrangement, control mechanisms, and strategies for minimizing decoherence – a primary challenge in quantum computing. The theoretical framework explores the potential acceleration achievable through QRAM in deep neural network training, with the primary goal of dramatically reducing training times. We present a detailed mathematical model outlining the data encoding process, quantum access protocols, and the expected performance gains. The architecture incorporates error mitigation techniques and discusses the scalability of the design for increasingly complex datasets. The research highlights the transformative potential of QRAM in accelerating ML, addressing a fundamental constraint within the current landscape of computational learning.

This research proposes a Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) architecture designed to overcome this limitation by leveraging quantum mechanical principles. The core concept involves encoding data into qubits and utilizing quantum random access to achieve near-instantaneous data retrieval. This paper details a novel QRAM architecture, focusing on qubit arrangement, control mechanisms, and strategies for minimizing decoherence – a primary challenge in quantum computing. The theoretical framework explores the potential acceleration achievable through QRAM in deep neural network training, with the primary goal of dramatically reducing training times. We present a detailed mathematical model outlining the data encoding process, quantum access protocols, and the expected performance gains. The architecture incorporates error mitigation techniques and discusses the scalability of the design for increasingly complex datasets. The research highlights the transformative potential of QRAM in accelerating ML, addressing a fundamental constraint within the current landscape of computational learning.

abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to probability graph computation based on an adaptive dynamic probability graph. Traditional methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their ability to effectively handle complex data and varying input conditions. This work introduces a dynamic algorithm that automatically adjusts probability graph parameters based on internal error and data characteristics, leading to improved accuracy and computational efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and experimental validation, showcasing a significant enhancement in prediction performance compared to existing methods. The core mechanism involves a self-adaptive parameter adjustment process driven by error estimation and data-specific analysis.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Quantum Error Correction Code Design
abstract: This paper proposes a dynamic adaptive quantum error correction (QEC) code design framework. The core idea is to leverage machine learning techniques to analyze error patterns during quantum information transmission and dynamically adjust the parameters of the QEC code accordingly. Traditional QEC codes are often designed with fixed parameters, which may not be optimal for all transmission scenarios. This adaptive approach aims to improve the robustness and reliability of quantum information transfer by tailoring the code to the specific characteristics of the channel and the data being transmitted. The system utilizes a feedback loop, where the machine learning model continuously learns from observed errors and adjusts the code's parameters to minimize error rates. This research addresses the critical need for more flexible and efficient QEC strategies in the development of practical quantum communication networks. The proposed framework offers a pathway towards significantly enhanced quantum information transmission performance.

title: Quantum-Inspired Data Structures for Parallel Computing
abstract: Quantum-inspired data structures offer a novel approach to parallel computing by utilizing the principles of quantum mechanics, particularly superposition and entanglement, to optimize the execution of computational tasks. This paper investigates the design and potential benefits of such data structures, aiming to achieve exponential speedups in certain computational scenarios. The core claim is that these data structures can significantly enhance the efficiency of parallel computations through a fundamentally different algorithmic approach. We explore the mathematical underpinnings of these structures and present preliminary results demonstrating their potential to outperform existing classical data structures under specific conditions. This work represents a significant step towards harnessing the power of quantum phenomena for parallel processing, offering a potentially transformative paradigm in computational efficiency.

title: ##可解释性人工智能的因果图推导 (KAIETP)
abstract: This paper introduces the KAIETP (Causal Inference for Explainable AI) framework, a novel approach to analyzing and interpreting the inner workings of explainable AI (XAI) models. Traditional XAI methods often focus on post-hoc explanations without fundamentally addressing the underlying causal relationships driving model decisions. KAIETP leverages causal inference theory to systematically decompose XAI models into their constituent causal structures, represented as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). These DAGs are then analyzed using causal reasoning algorithms to identify and quantify the key causal pathways responsible for the model's predictions. The core contribution lies in providing a structured, theoretically grounded method for understanding the 'why' behind XAI model outputs, ultimately enhancing interpretability and trust. This framework moves beyond simply highlighting correlations and instead focuses on establishing genuine causal links. The presented methodology offers a robust foundation for debugging, improving, and ultimately, building more reliable and transparent AI systems. This paper details the KAIETP framework, outlining the key steps involved in DAG construction, causal reasoning, and the interpretation of the resulting causal relationships.

title: Quantum Computing Breakthroughs and Renewed Investments
abstract: Quantum computing has entered an era of extraordinary progress, following the development of scalable architectures, noise-resilient algorithms, and compiler optimizations. This article describes how a new wave of international investment is driving the development of quantum hardware and software ranging from systems based on superconductors and on-property, to ion trap systems. We examine the connection between funding and practical impact (including recent progress towards fault-tolerant computing for real-world tasks). Combing the performance metrics with the innovation trends, the study paves the way for academia, industry, and policymakers to realize quantum advantage by using a more efficient approach.

title: A compression ratio estimation and optimization algorithm based on multi-modal feature fusion and hierarchical matching
abstract: The accurate estimation of differential compression ratio is pivotal to enhancing data storage and transmission efficiency. To overcome the three shortcomings of the traditional EDCR(efficient delta compression ratio) framework: high feature collision rate(>12%), low matching efficiency(the average time consumption per match is 4.0 ms) and inadequate dynamic adaptability, this paper proposes a novel optimization algorithm based on multimodal feature fusion and hierarchical matching architecture. The novelty includes: 128 bit composite feature values that integrate the Adler-32 rolling Hash, SHA-256 fingerprint and entropy-based type tag are established; the three-tier hierarchical matching architecture that includes the Bloom filter, the Hash table and the Jaccard fuzzy matching is designed; the time-decay dynamic redundancy model and the exponential smoothing calibration mechanism are set up. The experiments with the VMA and RDB(virtual machine image and redis database) real datasets demonstrate that: ①In the high-redundancy phase (redundancy>40%), the mean error of compression ratio estimation is reduced to 2.1% and 86.3% higher than the EDCR algorithm. ②The error is as low as 2.4% when the noise level is 31 and the noise resistance is 85.8% higher. ③The time consumption for feature computation decreases from 4.0 ms to 0.4 ms (90% decrease) and the matching frequency is 85% lower. ④The throughput increases by 23.4% to 34.4% on the SSD medium. This paper provides a high-precision and low-latency compression ratio estimation framework for a massive data system, satisfying the high-performance requirements for cloud storage and edge computing scenes.

title: Fine-grained Distributed Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning, as a privacy-preserving distributed machine learning paradigm, faces significant threats from backdoor attacks. Compared to centralized attacks, distributed backdoor attacks are more harmful but require more poisoned samples to compensate for the loss of trigger strength due to decomposition. Fixed trigger patterns are also easily detected by robust aggregation algorithms, increasing the risk of attack exposure. To address these challenges, we propose a fine-grained distributed backdoor attack framework (FDBA). This framework uses dynamic trigger generation and embedding vector optimization to perform attacks with fewer poisoned samples. First, we design a dynamic trigger generation method based on image edge structures using the Canny algorithm to extract edge features, which are then injected with Laplacian noise. RGB channel decomposition is applied for covert adaptation of the distributed trigger, reducing detection chances. Second, we introduce an embedding vector contrastive learning strategy that forces poisoned samples to approach the target class center in the feature space, enhancing attack effectiveness. On CIFAR-10, piecewise-linear estimates for target ASRs between 70\% and 90\% show that FDBA reduces the required poisoning ratio by 37.4\%--48.4\% compared with DBA. In non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) scenarios, FDBA retains 84.7\% of its IID attack performance under extreme heterogeneity, whereas DBA drops to 73.5\%, and the framework successfully bypasses mainstream defense mechanisms. This study offers new insights into federated learning security and emphasizes the potential threats and defense challenges posed by fine-grained distributed attacks.

title: Risk Is Not Review Value: Wrong-Answer Exposure Under Bounded Review Budgets
abstract: LLM assistants often produce more answers than humans can review before users see them. Most evaluations ask whether an answer is wrong, unsupported, or low-confidence. Bounded review budgets instead ask which answers should be checked first under a fixed review budget. Risk alone is not enough: a high-risk answer may be hard to repair, while a moderately risky answer may be directly correctable from available evidence. For generated-answer evaluation, we model review prioritization as exposure reduction, where review value combines estimated wrongness, intervention affordance, impact, and cost. We evaluate review queues with Wrong-Answer Exposure Ratio (WAER), the fraction of wrong answers left unreviewed, and post-repair residual exposure (PRRE), the fraction still exposed after deterministic benchmark-supported repairs. PRRE uses repairability rules that do not numerically reuse the affordance scores used for ranking. On a 720-item TAT-QA/SciFact stress benchmark, review-value ranking keeps answer-level WAER nearly unchanged at 20% budget (0.605 vs. 0.600) but lowers PRRE from 0.881 to 0.716. These results show that trustworthy LLM evaluation should measure not only error detection, but also how limited review capacity reduces exposed wrong answers.

title: Geometric Reliability of Neural Population Codes: Sampling Calibration and Within-Session Nonstationarity
abstract: Trial-to-trial variability limits how reliably neural population geometry can be estimated, while comparisons across populations depend on neuron and trial counts, response quality, and clustered sampling. We quantified within-session geometric reliability using Shesha, the Spearman correlation between representational dissimilarity matrices estimated from independent trial subsets, in all 39 Steinmetz Neuropixels sessions and in olfactory bulb and piriform cortex recordings from Bolding and Franks. Steinmetz analyses matched neurons and repetitions, compared observed reliability with a stationary residual-bootstrap expectation, and used mouse-level or mouse-clustered inference. Mean matched reliability was 0.0402 across 312 area-by-session recordings. Regional differences and reliability above the stationary benchmark did not survive correction. Temporal effects received the strongest support: interleaving early and late trials increased reliability relative to blocked allocation (Δ=0.02666, q=0.001953), and RDM similarity declined with within-session lag (mean mouse-level slope =-0.01912, q=0.001953; n=10 mice). Outer-cross-fitted reliability was not associated with choice-direction coupling or stimulus or response-direction decoding after correction. Olfactory comparisons remained descriptive because few paired sessions and no animal identities were available. In held-out simulations, associative recurrence outperformed feedforward subspace denoising but not divisive normalization. Representational geometry became less reproducible with temporal separation within a session, and comparisons across neural populations require sampling calibration and independent inference.

title: Cross-database transportability of a parsimonious postoperative ICU mortality model: Code and reproducibility materials
abstract: This repository contains analysis code and reproducibility materials supporting the study “Cross-database transportability of a parsimonious postoperative ICU mortality model: external evaluation of care-group information from MIMIC-IV to INSPIRE.” The release includes cohort-construction and harmonization scripts, model specifications, preprocessing parameters, feature and outcome definitions, aggregate results, software environment specifications, and provenance and file-integrity records. The analyses used MIMIC-IV version 3.1 and INSPIRE version 1.4.2. Patient-level source data are not included in this public release. Re-execution of patient-level analyses requires authorized access to the source databases, compliance with the applicable data-use agreements, and appropriate local configuration. Release version: 1.0.0. Licensing: Original analysis code is released under the MIT License. Documentation and original aggregate materials are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. Third-party materials retain their original licenses. These licenses do not apply to the restricted source datasets.

title: Post-benchmark analysis package: label-free observability of silent EHR pipeline failures (code, locked real-event registry, decision log #93–#112; git 6bb4ad7)
abstract: Preregistered, frozen protocol package for a controlled information-ablation benchmark of label-free observability of silent failures in electronic health record (EHR) data pipelines. The package contains the frozen protocol (v1.0, 2026-08-14) and its v1.1 addendum, the frozen failure-mechanism taxonomy, observables registry and pipeline DAG node table, the complete decision log with every entry annotated as to whether comparative results had been seen, a scope-boundary declaration, substrate qualification reports for eICU-CRD v2.0 (primary substrate) and MIMIC-IV v3.1 (portability substrate), a bilingual inventory of the public data actually used (metadata and SHA-256 fingerprints only), a code snapshot, and the benchmark-evaluation-start record. This deposit was made before the formal benchmark was run. As of deposit, no detection, localisation or paired-gain results had been computed. The code state is anchored by git commit 019af8d and code-snapshot digest dd99b59e930342daa4728276cff774e1ec0860802d28c143a8ddaf043f21ee4e. No patient-level data are included. eICU-CRD and MIMIC-IV are available from PhysioNet under their respective data use agreements. Manuscript text is not included.Version note (relative to protocol-v1.1-frozen, git 019af8d): core.Pipeline gained an instance-level ctx_extra dictionary so that the cohort literal and unit-conversion bindings declared in decision log entries #78 and #79 can reach node contexts (entry #82, recorded in the deviations register); four run parameters not fixed by the protocol — the matched empirical false-alarm rate α, the reference-window definition, the base-window positions, and the localisation-metric denominator — were prespecified (entry #83); and the code snapshot and benchmark-evaluation-start record were regenerated against git commit 7b6b5f2. No data, no substrate qualification decision, and no frozen taxonomy, DAG, observables registry or estimand definition were changed. As of this deposit no comparative results had been computed.

title: Self-Organizing Neural Networks: Dynamic Entropy Control
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic entropy control algorithm for self-organizing neural networks (SONNs). SONNs are a type of neural network architecture characterized by a dynamic and adaptive structure, allowing for flexible representation and improved generalization. The core of this algorithm lies in a carefully orchestrated adjustment of network entropy, influencing the network's internal representation and ultimately affecting its learning performance. Traditional methods often rely on fixed parameters, while this approach leverages entropy as a mechanism for continuous learning and improved robustness. We present a rigorous theoretical analysis and practical implementation of this algorithm, demonstrating its potential to enhance both the expressiveness and learning capabilities of SONNs. The research explores the impact of entropy distribution on network stability and convergence.

title: Title: Universal Quantum State Representation
abstract: Quantum State Representation (QSR) is a novel formalism for representing quantum states, designed to facilitate efficient computation and communication across diverse quantum platforms. This paper introduces a 'Quantum Hierarchical State Space' – a layered network structuring quantum states – to enhance algorithm design and computational efficiency. We demonstrate the benefits of this structure through a rigorous analysis of key quantum algorithms, highlighting its potential to overcome current limitations in quantum software development. The core mechanism involves organizing states into a hierarchical system, allowing for targeted computation and improved algorithmic adaptability. This represents a significant step towards a more unified and versatile approach to quantum computing, offering a potential bridge between established paradigms.

title: Self-Organizing Neural Networks for Quantum State Tomography
abstract: Quantum state tomography (QST) is a fundamental technique in quantum information science, used to characterize the density matrix of an unknown quantum state. However, traditional QST methods are often computationally intensive, requiring a large number of measurements and sophisticated data analysis techniques. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing self-organizing neural networks (SONNs) for direct quantum state reconstruction. The core idea is to train a SONN to learn the mapping between experimental measurement data and the corresponding density matrix, thereby bypassing the need for precise control over the quantum system and significantly reducing the computational burden. We detail the architecture of the SONN, the training process, and demonstrate the potential of this method to achieve accurate state reconstruction with fewer measurements. The proposed method offers a promising path towards more efficient and scalable QST, particularly for complex quantum systems.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning with Semantic Web Technologies
abstract: This paper explores the integration of neural networks and symbolic reasoning through the application of Semantic Web technologies. The core challenge in neuro-symbolic reasoning lies in effectively bridging the gap between the representation learning capabilities of neural networks and the explicit knowledge representation and inference mechanisms of symbolic systems. We propose a framework that leverages Semantic Web technologies, specifically OWL (Web Ontology Language) and RDF (Resource Description Framework), to provide a structured knowledge base and rules, which are then integrated with neural networks to facilitate neuro-symbolic reasoning and inference. This approach aims to overcome the limitations of purely neural or purely symbolic systems by combining their respective strengths. The paper details the architecture of the proposed system, outlining the data flow between the neural network and the semantic reasoning engine. We demonstrate the potential of this integrated approach through a conceptual example and discuss future research directions, focusing on scalability, robustness, and the development of more sophisticated mechanisms for translating between the two paradigms. The key contribution is the systematic approach to combining these technologies, offering a pathway toward more reliable and explainable AI systems.

title: Geometry Topology Quantum Computing Simulation
abstract: This paper presents a novel system for simulating complex geometric structures utilizing the unique capabilities of quantum computing. Traditional computational methods often struggle to accurately model quantum phenomena due to the inherent complexity of quantum systems. Quantum computing offers the potential for significantly enhanced precision in these simulations. We propose a system that leverages quantum algorithms to mimic intricate geometric structures, providing a framework for advanced simulation and analysis. The core of this work lies in the design of a 'Geometric Topology Quantum Computing Simulation' system, focusing on precise representation and manipulation of geometric data. The system aims to surpass the limitations of classical simulation techniques in modeling complex geometries, offering a pathway to new insights in areas such as materials science, cryptography, and theoretical physics. We detail the system's architecture, the underlying quantum algorithms employed, and a preliminary demonstration of its capabilities.

title: Quantum Topological Bifurcation Structures: A Novel Approach to Topology and Cryptography
abstract: This paper explores the intersection of quantum topology and cryptography, focusing on the development of novel quantum topological bifurcation structures. We investigate how these structures, rooted in quantum mechanics, can encode and manipulate information, potentially leading to enhanced cryptographic security. The core of our research lies in defining a specific mathematical framework—a topological bifurcation structure—that intrinsically incorporates quantum properties. We demonstrate the feasibility of analyzing these structures using topological information theory, revealing intricate relationships between the structure's geometry and the underlying quantum dynamics. Furthermore, we propose a new algorithm for generating and analyzing these structures, offering potential advancements in secure communication protocols. The study highlights the unique capabilities of these structures, emphasizing their potential impact on both quantum computing and cryptographic security.

title: Distributed Proof-Checking via Probabilistic Theorem Proving on Graph-Structured Data
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to automated theorem proving and proof verification, termed distributed proof-checking, which leverages probabilistic theorem proving (PTP) techniques applied to graph-structured mathematical data. The core challenge in traditional theorem proving lies in its inherent computational expense, particularly when dealing with complex theorems and lengthy proofs. Our approach addresses this limitation by representing mathematical theorems and their corresponding proofs as graphs. These graphs encapsulate logical relationships, dependencies, and structural components of the proof. Probabilistic theorem proving algorithms are then applied to these graph representations to automatically verify the correctness of the proof. Crucially, we propose a distributed computing architecture to scale the proof-checking process, exploiting parallel processing capabilities to significantly reduce verification time. This paper details the framework, outlines the key components, and discusses the potential benefits of this approach, positioning it as a significant advancement in the field of automated reasoning. We demonstrate how graph-based reasoning provides a more efficient and scalable foundation for theorem proving compared to traditional, symbolic methods. The core of our method is the application of PTP to a graph representation of a proof, allowing for probabilistic certainty in the verification process.

title: Title: Dynamic Probability Distribution Machine Learning Model with Automated Parameter Adjustment
abstract: This paper presents a novel machine learning model leveraging dynamic probability distributions as its core parameter. Traditional machine learning models often require retraining to adapt to evolving data distributions, presenting a significant challenge. Our approach introduces a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism that automatically adjusts model parameters based on the changing distribution of the input data. This allows for a more adaptive and robust learning process, effectively addressing the limitations of static models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through a series of experiments on various benchmark datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve superior performance compared to traditional methods in scenarios with fluctuating data. The core mechanism focuses on a probabilistic weighting scheme, allowing the model to prioritize relevant features based on the current data distribution.

title: Efficient Optimization on the Euclidean Sphere: Riemannian Gradient Alignment as a Unifying Principle
abstract: Euclidean sphere-constrained optimization problems represent perhaps the most basic class of nonconvex-constrained problems for which there exist efficient optimization algorithms for specific problem instances, such as the eigenvalue problems and learning problems arising in the recent literature. However, when and why we can efficiently optimize on the sphere using simple first-order methods is poorly understood. We introduce Riemannian Gradient Alignment (RGA) as a unifying structural condition enabling fast convergence. RGA is a parameterized directional error bound requiring a tangent vector to sufficiently align with a target solution vector. We prove that Riemannian Gradient Descent with diminishing step sizes converges linearly when RGA holds with order $r=1$, and at rate $O(k^{-1/(2r-2)})$ for $r>1$. The result applies even to tangent vector fields that are not gradients of any objective. Our main technical contribution is a family of derivative-based sufficient conditions for RGA. We prove these conditions for a range of learning problems, including multi-instance learning/max pooling, Gaussian halfspaces, single-index and generalized linear models, phase retrieval, complete orthogonal dictionary learning, and (sparse) PCA. The provided examples span distributional families that include standard Gaussian, conditionally Gaussian, and more general structured distributions. The provided guarantees cover objectives that are generally not (geodesically) convex, may be nonsmooth, and may arise from discrete distributions. These results establish tractability of problem classes where no prior error bound conditions were known, as well as unify, strengthen, and generalize several prior results.

title: NeuCME: Toward Dynamic Multimodal Continual Learning via Neural Combinatorics of Multiple Experts
abstract: Multimodal continual learning has recently shown great potential for developing agents with human-like intelligence by continuously learning new tasks across multiple modalities. However, existing methods typically assume that the set of modalities per task is predefined and fixed. In this paper, we investigate a more realistic learning setting, referred to as dynamic multimodal continual learning, in which the set of modalities may vary across tasks rather than remaining fixed. This setting involves two primary challenges: (i) spatio-temporal catastrophic forgetting and (ii) adaptive multimodal fusion. To address these challenges, we propose NeuCME (as shorthand for \textbf{Neu}ral \textbf{C}ombinatorics of \textbf{M}ultiple \textbf{E}xperts), a novel framework designed to effectively learn and integrate knowledge across tasks with varying modalities. The proposed NeuCME model comprises three key components, namely modality-combinational rehearsal, multi-gated mixture-of-experts, and task relevance-guided distillation. Furthermore, we formulate an evaluation metric to quantify the dynamism of task sequences and then set up a comprehensive benchmark with different degrees of dynamism. Extensive experiments using four real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed NeuCME outperforms state-of-the-art methods markedly.

title: An Efficient Metric for Data Quality Measurement in Imitation Learning
abstract: Imitation learning (IL) has seen remarkable progress, yet field deployment of IL-powered robots remains hindered by the challenge of out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Fine-tuning pre-trained policies with end-user demonstrations collected in deployment environments is a promising strategy to address this challenge. However, end-user demonstrations are frequently of poor quality, characterized by excessive corrective motions, oscillations, and abrupt adjustments that degrade both learned and fine-tuned policy performance. Existing automated approaches for curating demonstration data require policy rollouts in the environment, making them computationally expensive and impractical for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose a fast, efficient, and fully automated demonstration ranking metric based on the power spectral density (PSD) of demonstration trajectories. The PSD metric requires no policy learning, environment interaction, or expert labeling, making it well-suited for scalable, in-the-field data curation. Lower PSD values correspond to smoother, higher-quality demonstrations, while higher PSD values indicate erratic, artifact-laden trajectories. We evaluate the proposed metric on two benchmark imitation learning datasets comprising expert and lay-user demonstrations, and through a user study with older adults at a retirement facility, where collected demonstrations are used to fine-tune pi0.5 intelligence2025pi_ for a daily living task. Results demonstrate that PSD-curated data yields policies with higher task success rates and smoother execution trajectories compared to uncurated baselines and two competitive data-ranking methods.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction (QCES) – Faster Solution for Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of Quantum Annealing (QA) to accelerate the solution of complex optimization problems, particularly those encountered in areas like logistics, resource allocation, and chemical synthesis. We propose a novel approach, Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction (QCES), which leverages the strengths of QA to efficiently solve optimization problems by integrating it with traditional constraint satisfaction techniques. The core mechanism involves a hybrid algorithm that combines the advantages of both quantum annealing and constraint satisfaction, demonstrating a significant reduction in computational time compared to conventional methods. The paper details the architecture of the QCES system, explores its performance through simulations, and discusses potential future research directions.

title: Probability Topological Neural Network Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel neural network optimization algorithm based on probability topology, aiming to enhance the adaptability of neural networks to complex and noisy data. The core concept centers on representing the network's topology as a probability distribution, which serves as a guiding principle for the optimization process. abstract: This paper explores the application of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) for robot control in complex environments. title: Quantum Accelerated Simulated Annealing
abstract: Simulated annealing (SA) is a widely used metaheuristic algorithm for solving optimization problems. However, its performance is often limited by the slow exploration of the search space. This paper explores the potential of accelerating simulated annealing using quantum computing. We propose a framework where the search space of SA is mapped to the quantum state space, leveraging quantum superposition and interference to expedite the search for the global optimum. The core claim is that quantum computation can significantly speed up the search process within simulated annealing. The mechanism relies on utilizing quantum algorithms to explore the solution space far more efficiently than classical methods. This work introduces a novel approach to optimization, demonstrating the potential of harnessing quantum mechanical phenomena to enhance the performance of classical optimization algorithms. The theoretical framework and conceptual design are presented, outlining a possible architecture for a quantum-accelerated simulated annealing system. The potential speedup is analyzed, and future research directions are discussed.

title: TT-G42 Cryptosystem
abstract: Abstract This paper presents the TT-G42 cryptosystem as described in the supplied technical materials. TT-G42 is a proposed software cryptosystem that combines hybrid classical/postquantum key establishment, authenticated session encryption, a geometric validation layer based on the 248-dimensional adjoint representation of E8, dual-source entropy collection, and continuously monitored runtime controls. The design uses NTRU-family or ML-KEM-style post-quantum components together with X25519, derives session material through a hash-based combiner, and protects application data with AES-GCM. A crystalwand sensor is proposed as an auxiliary physical entropy source whose telemetry is healthtested and mixed with operating-system entropy before deterministic random-bit generation. title: 自适应几何数据结构的基于图的概率建模框架
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for probabilistic data structure modeling based on graph structures. Traditional probabilistic modeling often relies on manual design of structural parameters, making it challenging to accommodate dynamic changes in data structures. Our approach leverages the inherent properties of graph structures to automatically generate and adjust graph parameters, enabling high-precision data structure modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through the application of a synthetic dataset with a complex, evolving structure. The core mechanism centers around a graph-based probabilistic model that adapts to the data's unique characteristics, ensuring robust and accurate representation. The resulting system offers a significant advancement over existing approaches by automating the structural design process, ultimately leading to more adaptable and insightful data modeling.

title: Contextualized Memory Networks for Embodied AI
abstract: Embodied AI agents face the significant challenge of learning and adapting within complex, dynamic environments. Traditional memory networks often struggle to effectively represent and utilize information when the context shifts, leading to suboptimal performance. This paper proposes a novel approach – Contextualized Memory Networks – designed to address this limitation. The core idea is to dynamically adapt memory storage and retrieval by associating each memory slot with a context vector. This allows the network to prioritize and retrieve memories that are most relevant to the agent's current situation, significantly improving learning and adaptation capabilities. We introduce a framework where the context vector, denoted as *ci*, represents the agent's perception of its environment at the time the memory *si* is stored. The retrieval process then utilizes a similarity function, *sim(ct, si)*, where *ct* is the current context vector, to determine the relevance of each memory *si* to the current time step *t*. The system employs a weighted average of retrieved memories based on their similarity scores, providing a context-aware memory access mechanism. This approach offers a substantial improvement over static memory networks by directly incorporating context awareness into the memory architecture, ultimately enhancing the agent's ability to learn and generalize in dynamic environments. The key contribution lies in the dynamic adjustment of memory prioritization based on real-time contextual information. The framework is amenable to various embodied AI applications, including navigation, manipulation, and interaction.

title: 基于量子纠缠的概率论验证算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel probabilistic verification algorithm predicated on the principles of quantum entanglement. Traditional probabilistic verification methods often struggle with the complexities of high-dimensional probability distributions, necessitating computationally intensive methods. This work explores the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement to enhance verification accuracy and reduce computational complexity. We introduce a new algorithm, termed "Entangled Verification," which leverages entangled states to establish a stronger correlation between input data and the model's output, leading to improved verification results. The core mechanism centers around creating and manipulating entangled states to quantify the model's behavior, offering a fundamentally different approach to probabilistic validation. We provide a detailed mathematical framework, including a formal analysis of the entanglement process and a preliminary validation of the algorithm's effectiveness on benchmark datasets. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential implications of this approach and outlines future research directions.

title: Title: Bayesian Non-Linear Differential Geometry for Algorithmic Stability
abstract: This paper investigates the use of Bayesian non-linear differential geometry as a means to enhance the stability and robustness of geometric algorithms. Traditional approaches frequently suffer from sensitivity to initial conditions and parameter choices, leading to divergent behavior. We propose a Bayesian framework that dynamically adjusts the geometry and constraints of differential geometry algorithms in real-time, based on data-driven uncertainty estimates and environmental conditions. The core mechanism involves Bayesian inference to continuously update the geometry and constraints, effectively mitigating instability and guaranteeing consistent results across diverse datasets. This research addresses a critical challenge in computational geometry, offering a novel approach to algorithmic stability through adaptive geometric modeling.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for Cross-Border Data Flows in Uganda: Robustness Under Distribution Shift and Sparse Labels
abstract: Cross-border data flows are central to Uganda's digital economy, yet their governance is complicated by competing pressures: the need for international integration and the legal obligation to protect citizen privacy. Federated learning offers a promising architecture for training machine learning models across distributed data custodians without centralising raw data. However, the practical viability of federated systems in this context is threatened by two statistical phenomena: distribution shift between participating nodes and extreme label sparsity. We introduce a generalised notion of client heterogeneity and derive convergence bounds for a FedAvg-style algorithm with differential privacy guarantees, showing that convergence degrades gracefully with increasing heterogeneity and privacy budget. We then propose a semi-supervised augmentation strategy that leverages the structure of unlabelled data to mitigate label sparsity, and we analyse its interaction with privacy mechanisms. The analysis reveals that the dominant design constraint is not communication cost but the joint effect of privacy noise and distribution skew on model bias. We conclude with design principles for federated systems operating in data-governance environments such as Uganda's, where legal fragmentation and infrastructural asymmetry are defining features.

title: ASTER and Sentinel-2MSI remote sensing data for mapping iron oxide-bearing zones, the case of Central Afghanistan
abstract: This study maps iron oxide–bearing zones in the northern Markazi Behsud District of Wardak Province, Central Afghanistan, using a comparative analysis of ASTER and Sentinel‑2 MSI data. Multiple remote sensing techniques, False Color Composites (FCC), Band Ratios (BR), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), the Crosta method, and the Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM), were applied to identify iron oxides and discriminate minerals such as magnetite, hematite, and goethite. This study newly established band ratios based on mineral spectral properties enhanced detection performance. The newly established spectral ratios, derived explicitly from diagnostic ferric and ferrous absorption features, differ from conventional band ratio schemes by offering improved sensitivity to iron‑bearing mineral variations and more robust delineation of hydrothermal alteration zones in multispectral data. Sentinel‑2 MSI produced markedly superior results compared to ASTER due to its higher spatial resolution and seamless single‑tile coverage. Among all methods, the Crosta technique and SAM were the most effective, with SAM showing the strongest agreement with USGS permissive mineralization zones. The integrated results delineate a continuous iron‑bearing belt approximately 54 km long and 6.8 km wide along the Baba Mountains. The overall accuracy of 71.3% demonstrates the strong capability of Sentinel‑2 MSI, particularly when combined with SAM, for mapping iron oxide–rich zones in structurally complex terrains.

title: LLM Agents as Computational Typologists
abstract: Linguistic typology relies on expert analysis of reference grammars across languages, making large-scale crosslinguistic comparison labor-intensive and unscalable. We introduce AUTOTYPOLOGIST, an LLM agent for evidence-grounded typological analysis over reference grammars. The agent is capable of retrieving relevant grammar sections, analyzing interlinear glossed text (IGT), and iteratively reasoning over typological hypotheses using a ReAct-style workflow. We evaluate the system on TYPOLOGICAL FEATURE CODING against expert annotations and TYPOLOGICAL HYPOTHESIS TESTING with typological universals using 25 open-source reference grammars. Operating under different information constraints in TYPOLOGICAL FEATURE CODING, the agent can synthesize information from reference grammar prose but still faces challenges with only IGTs in the target language. In TYPOLOGICAL HYPOTHESIS TESTING, the agent can synthesize crosslinguistic evidence and identify both supporting cases and counterexamples. These findings suggest that LLM agents can support scalable and inspectable typological analysis, while still requiring expert validation.

title: From Simulated Citizens to Simulated Deliberation: Challenges in Representation and Interaction
abstract: Can LLM agents simulate how a real public would deliberate? For such simulations to be meaningful, agents must reflect the population's opinions, and their views must be shaped by what others say during discussion. We evaluate these requirements across six LLMs using national surveys, controlled deliberation experiments, and a real deliberative poll. Comparing census-grounded Korean personas against national surveys, we find that agents often produce overly concentrated opinions and fail to reliably reproduce demographic differences. During simulated deliberation, agents exchange arguments, respond to one another, and frequently change positions. Yet similar changes occur even when agents cannot see one another's contributions, while simply restating their starting positions sharply reduces movement. We further test whether these limitations persist in a real-world setting, using agents constructed from actual respondents in the 2017 Shin-Kori deliberative poll. Even with real respondent profiles, agents fail to reproduce the panel's initial opinion distribution or how its opinions change across survey waves. evidence.title: From Simulated Citizens to Simulated Deliberation: Challenges in Representation and Interaction
evidence.abstract: Can LLM agents simulate how a real public would deliberate? For such simulations to be meaningful, agents must reflect the population's opinions, and their views must be shaped by what others say during discussion. We evaluate these requirements across six LLMs using national surveys, controlled deliberation experiments, and a real deliberative poll. Comparing census-grounded Korean personas against national surveys, we find that agents often produce overly concentrated opinions and fail to reliably reproduce demographic differences. During simulated deliberation, agents exchange arguments, respond to one another, and frequently change positions. Yet similar changes occur even when agents cannot see one another's contributions, while simply restating their starting positions sharply reduces movement. We further test whether these limitations persist in a real-world setting, using agents constructed from actual respondents in the 2017 Shin-Kori deliberative poll. Even with real respondent profiles, agents fail to reproduce the panel's initial opinion distribution or how its opinions change across survey waves. Our findings show that generating deliberative discussions, representing public opinion, and reproducing interaction-driven opinion change are distinct capabilities. These results suggest a different potential role for LLM deliberation: surfacing arguments and perspectives, rather than simulating a real public.

title: Qubit-Based Benchmarking of InP HEMT LNAs: Readout Fidelity Versus Power Consumption
abstract: High-fidelity single-shot readout of superconducting qubits is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Without a quantum-limited amplifier such as a Josephson parametric amplifier, the cryogenic high-electron-mobility-transistor (HEMT) low-noise amplifier (LNA) at the 4 K stage is the dominant noise source in the readout chain. HEMT LNAs are conventionally characterized by Y-factor measurements of the noise temperature $T_N$, independently of the quantum measurement they ultimately serve. Here we present a qubit-in-the-loop benchmarking method. The method uses the two-dimensional IQ histogram of single-shot readout as a direct figure of merit. We apply it to three state-of-the-art cryogenic InP HEMT LNAs with 53\%, 60\%, and 70\% channel indium content, together with a commercial reference amplifier. The 60\% and 70\% devices have similar $T_N$ in Y-factor measurements, both lower than the 53\% device. The 70\% device has the highest gain, but qubit readout SNR and assignment fidelity $\mathcal{F}_a$ instead peak at 60\%. Using this method, we map $\mathcal{F}_a$ against HEMT LNA dc power consumption for each device. $\mathcal{F}_a$ does not simply saturate with increasing power. For several devices it declines above a device-dependent power well below typical operating points. For the 60\% device, which has the highest overall $\mathcal{F}_a$, about 1~mW is needed to maintain $\mathcal{F}_a > 85\%$. Across all four devices, $\mathcal{F}_a > 80\%$ is reached with as little as about 0.3~mW, roughly an order of magnitude below typical operating points. These results establish a qubit-referenced benchmarking methodology and provide practical guidance for amplifier selection and bias in power-constrained multi-qubit readout systems.

title: SQS: Bayesian DNN Compression through Sparse Quantized Sub-distributions
abstract: Compressing large-scale neural networks is essential for deploying models on resource-constrained devices. Most existing methods adopt weight pruning or low-bit quantization individually, often resulting in suboptimal compression rates to preserve acceptable performance drops. We introduce a unified framework for simultaneous pruning and low-bit quantization via Bayesian variational learning (\method), which achieves higher compression rates than prior baselines while maintaining comparable performance. The key idea is to employ a spike-and-slab prior to induce sparsity and model quantized weights using Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) to enable low-bit precision. Due to the intractability of the objective involving spike-and-slab priors with GMMs, we derive an efficient approximation that facilitates effective compression with minimal accuracy loss. In theory, we provide a consistent result for our proposed variational approach to a sparse and quantized deep neural network. Extensive experiments on compressing ResNet, BERT-base, Llama3.2, and Qwen2.5 models show that our method achieves higher compression rates than a line of existing methods with comparable performance drops. title: ANALYSIS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE'S VARIOUS DOMAIN
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a game-changer technology with potential applications in many sectors including healthcare, finance, education, manufacturing, transportation, agriculture, cyber security, retail, energy, and smart cities. The study examines key AI techniques and how they are applied in various fields, focusing on their advantages, drawbacks, and feasibility. The study covers supervised and unsupervised learning, semi-supervised learning, neural networks, deep learning, natural language processing, ensemble methods, fuzzy logic, expert systems and robotics. Literature review was done to gain insight into the development and cross-domain applications of AI, and comparative analysis was performed on the capabilities and challenges of various AI techniques. The results show that AI can enhance efficiency, automation, prediction, pattern recognition, and decision-making processes in various industries, but there are concerns and challenges associated with its use, such as data quality, privacy and security, ethics, transparency, cost, computational demand, and human involvement. The study also indicates that the appropriateness of the AI technique is dependent on the problem type, data properties and special application requirements. The study suggests that fostering a cross-domain perspective of AI can help in selecting the most suitable technique and promote responsible, effective, and human-centred AI adoption in various fields.

title: RCKH-LHS-kNN Reproducibility Package v1.0.4: EEJET Verification Supplement
abstract: This repository provides the reproducibility supplement for the study “Identification of Dataset- and Classifier-Dependent Performance Patterns in Latin Hypercube Sampling with Nearest-Neighbor Rebalancing for Imbalanced Classification.” The study investigates the dataset- and classifier-dependent behavior of a frozen RCKH-LHS-kNN rebalancing procedure across 20 public tabular datasets, eight sampling conditions, four classifier families, and five deterministic seeds. The primary analysis characterizes dataset-level benefit, neutral, and loss regimes relative to SMOTE and examines classifier-specific performance, structural dataset characteristics, minority-class outcomes, and computational cost. Version 1.0.4 provides the supporting materials required to trace and verify the results reported in the manuscript. The package includes the frozen experimental configuration, dataset manifests and provenance information, preprocessing specifications, fold-level outputs, dataset-by-classifier summaries, classification metrics, synthetic-sample audit records, statistical-analysis materials, source data for the reported tables and figures, manuscript-to-source value mappings, integrity checks, and reproducibility documentation. The frozen experimental observations and classifier outputs were not modified for this update, and no classifier was retrained. Version 1.0.4 primarily improves the organization, traceability, documentation, and consistency of the materials supporting the manuscript. Third-party datasets are redistributed only where their original licenses permit. Where redistribution is not permitted, the repository provides provenance and available access information, checksums, and preparation information to support reproducibility. Users are encouraged to consult the included README, dataset manifest, source tables, manuscript-value map, and verification documentation when reproducing or interpreting the reported results.

title: Title: Geometric Fractal Automata with Adaptive Constraints
abstract: Geometric Fractal Automata (GFAs) represent a novel approach to automated design, focusing on the evolution of fractal geometries guided by adaptive constraints. This paper explores the creation of GFAs, characterized by a "Genetic Constraint Engine" that governs the evolution of fractal structures. The core mechanism involves a population of automata, each possessing an internal state and dynamically adjusted constraints. This allows the system to explore a vast design space, responding to internal factors and external stimuli to generate complex and aesthetically pleasing fractal patterns. The research emphasizes the integration of adaptive constraints, moving beyond static design approaches to create systems capable of self-improvement and organic evolution within a defined framework. The paper details the implementation of the Genetic Constraint Engine, its parameters, and the resulting evolution of a simple GFAs, illustrating the potential of this approach for generating intricate and aesthetically compelling designs.

title: Title: Axiomatic Probability Space Modeling with Emergent Variables
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic modeling framework based on constraint propagation, designed to automatically generate new variables within a probability space. The core mechanism centers around iteratively refining variables by responding to existing variables and constraints, leading to the emergence of entirely new mathematical objects. Traditional probabilistic models often rely on predefined distributions; this approach aims to discover and generate variables directly from the underlying space. We explore the potential for this technique to produce unexpected and valuable mathematical structures, pushing the boundaries of probabilistic modeling. This work demonstrates the potential for automated discovery of novel mathematical concepts through the iterative generation of variables.

title: 基于动态量子态的概率模型
abstract: This paper presents a novel probabilistic model, termed the "Dynamic Quantum State-Based Probability Model," designed to predict and autonomously generate optimal strategies for complex system simulations. Traditional probabilistic models often struggle to effectively address complex environments due to their reliance on static parameters. This work introduces a method leveraging the dynamic evolution of quantum states to achieve enhanced predictive capabilities and automated strategic generation. We demonstrate the model's efficacy through illustrative examples, showcasing its ability to accurately forecast system behavior and generate optimal strategies across various simulated scenarios. The core of the model lies in its quantum state dynamics, which allows for a more nuanced and adaptable representation of system behavior compared to traditional approaches. This results in improved predictive accuracy and facilitates the automated generation of optimal strategies.

title: Differential Privacy for Federated Learning with Dynamic Group Membership
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to machine learning by enabling collaborative model training across decentralized devices without directly exchanging data. However, traditional FL methods often struggle to provide strong differential privacy guarantees, especially when group membership and data heterogeneity change dynamically. This paper proposes a novel framework for enhancing differential privacy in FL by incorporating a dynamic privacy budget allocation scheme. The core idea is to adapt the privacy level based on the size and diversity of each participating group, mitigating the impact of fluctuating group memberships and varying data distributions. We present a detailed analysis of the challenges posed by dynamic group membership and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a theoretical framework. The proposed method aims to strike a balance between model accuracy and privacy preservation, contributing to a more robust and reliable FL system. The key contributions lie in the adaptive privacy allocation and the addressing of non-static group dynamics.

title: 基于量子态的拓扑网络优化
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to topology network optimization utilizing quantum state manipulation. Traditional methods often rely on classical algorithms, but this research explores the potential of quantum mechanics to enhance network structure optimization. We propose a method that leverages the inherent properties of quantum states to represent and optimize network topologies, aiming to improve network performance. The core mechanism involves quantum algorithms designed to iteratively refine network configurations based on quantum state transformations. This offers a potential paradigm shift in topology network optimization, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical approaches. The study details the theoretical underpinnings of the proposed method, including the representation of networks using quantum states and the core algorithm design. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges and future directions for this research, emphasizing the potential for significant advancements in network design and performance.

title: Quantum Computing for Simulation of Complex Chemical Reactions
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum computing for simulating complex chemical reactions. Traditional classical computational methods often struggle with the inherent quantum mechanical nature of chemical systems, particularly when dealing with large molecules and intricate reaction pathways. This work proposes a novel quantum algorithm leveraging superposition and entanglement to directly simulate the time evolution of these systems. The core of the algorithm centers on a time-dependent Schrödinger equation (TDSE) implemented on a quantum computer. We outline the key elements, including the encoding of molecular states, the construction of a suitable Hamiltonian operator, and the execution of the quantum algorithm to obtain the final state of the system. The efficiency gains compared to classical methods, particularly for reactions involving significant quantum effects, are discussed. Furthermore, we highlight the potential impact of this technology on accelerating drug discovery, materials science, and fundamental chemical research. The algorithm's core relies on the ability of a quantum computer to perform a vast number of calculations simultaneously, offering a substantial advantage over classical computers when simulating quantum systems.
